objectives: Explain who Prophet Noah was.
Explain the title Prophets of Great Determination.
Say why Noah was sent to his people.
Use the passive and known for / as.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter gives the key facts: the title, the 71st surah, the Flood, the beginning of idolatry and the 950 years. A fact file (title → surah → mission → age → job) helps learners organize the information before reading the story itself.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Qur’an verses say Noah stayed with his people for 950 years; the chapter says it is not clear if this was his whole life.
Idolatry first appeared among Noah’s people; earlier generations believed in one Allah.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past simple passive · be known for / as · bear a name
Notice (Activity 1): His people were drowned in the Great Flood …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *known with · *were drown · *is known like.
Use (Activity 4): a person of determination.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: u-LU’L AZM, taw-HEED, AN-ka-but, ID-ris.
Stress: de-ter-mi-NA-tion, JUDG-ment, gen-er-A-tions.
beforeReading: Ask: “What does determination mean? Who do you know with strong determination?”
duringReading: First reading: Who was Prophet Noah?
Second reading: complete the fact file.
Find what is not clear about the 950 years.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Fact file; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a person of determination; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is Noah called a Prophet of Great Determination?
Why did Allah send Noah?
What three possibilities does the chapter give for the 950 years?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Ulu’l Azm” and “950 Years” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: determination, bears, name, judgment, generations, Idolatry, appeared, carpenter.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the fact file with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short encyclopedia entry about Prophet Noah with two passive sentences.

formativeAssessment: Uses the passive or known for correctly.
expectedResponses: Prophet Noah (pbuh) is known for his great determination. Idolatry first appeared among his people, so Allah sent him to guide them back to the belief in the Oneness of Allah.
content.transferTask: Write about a person known for determination.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the three possibilities about the 950 years as the book gives them?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “is known for” and one passive sentence.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses the passive or known for.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain in three sentences who Noah (pbuh) was and why Allah sent him. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraphs 1 and 2, B reads paragraph 3. Each explains the main idea and one detail. The partner asks one follow-up question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence after the verses. Asker asks “What is not clear about the 950 years?” Checker checks the three possibilities.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “Why is Noah (pbuh) one of the five great prophets?” The learner answers in two or three sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “For this reason, Allah sent Noah (pbuh) to turn his people away from idols and guide them back to the belief in the Oneness of Allah.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, who Noah (pbuh) was and why Allah sent him to his people. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer say ‘it is not clear’ about the 950 years?” (The sources do not say exactly which period it was.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the title, the number of the surah and the three possible meanings of the 950 years.

thinkAloud.sentence: However, it is not clear if this period was his whole life, his time as a prophet, or just the time before the flood.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “However” and “it is not clear” tell me the writer is careful. There are three possible answers, and the text does not choose one. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Idolatry first appeared among Noah’s people.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What appeared for the first time among Noah’s people?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: Why is determination important in a difficult task?

content.chapter: Chapter 2: The Flood in Ancient Stories
objectives: Summarize the Babylonian flood story.
Explain where the oldest flood stories come from.
Present the epic as an ancient account.
Use the present simple for a story summary.
content.pedagogy: The chapter shows that flood stories are found in ancient texts outside the Qur’an. Present the Epic of Gilgamesh as an ancient account, in the words of the book, without comparing or judging it. A story chain helps learners follow the epic.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The epic is an ancient Babylonian text; it is not the Qur’anic account.
Uta-napishtim is a character in the epic; Gilgamesh goes to find him.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: present simple for summaries · passive (were written, is told, is found)
Notice (Activity 1): Gilgamesh … is deeply sad … he goes on a journey.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *The flood last · *the story is tell.
Use (Activity 4): a story summary.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: GIL-ga-mesh, U-ruk, SU-mer, BAB-y-lon, u-ta-na-PISH-tim, E-a.
Stress: e-TER-nal, im-MOR-tal, DE-scrip-tion.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do you know any very old stories from other cultures?”
duringReading: First reading: Where do the oldest flood stories come from?
Second reading: complete the story chain.
Find why Gilgamesh goes on a journey.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Story chain; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a story summary; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does Gilgamesh want to find Uta-napishtim?
Who warns Uta-napishtim in the epic?
Why do you think many old cultures have flood stories?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Tablets” and “Gilgamesh” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: description, survived, immortal, eternal, epic, deeply.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the story chain with the first event written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a summary of the epic in six sentences in the present simple.

formativeAssessment: Says where the stories come from.
expectedResponses: The oldest flood stories come from tablets written in Sumer and Babylon. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, Gilgamesh goes to find Uta-napishtim, who survived the Flood and became immortal.
content.transferTask: Write a summary of a story or film you know.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners present the epic as an ancient account, without comparing?

exitTicket: Write one sentence in the present simple about the epic.

rubricLevels.secure: Says where the stories come from.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners retell the Babylonian flood story in four steps. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner why Gilgamesh went on a journey. The partner restates it with “because he wanted to”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentences about the flood in the epic. Listener notes how long it lasted. Writer writes where the ship landed.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A museum visitor looks at an old clay tablet and asks, “What story is this?” The learner explains in three sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The oldest flood stories come from ancient Middle Eastern tablets which were written in Sumer and Babylon.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the Epic of Gilgamesh tells about a great flood. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer include this chapter in a story about Noah (pbuh)?” (To show that many old peoples told stories about a great flood.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name Gilgamesh and Uta-napishtim and give the events in order.

thinkAloud.strategy: Follow a story inside a story
thinkAloud.sentence: So, he goes on a journey to find Uta-napishtim, who survived the Flood and became immortal.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: This is a story inside the epic. “So” shows the reason: Gilgamesh wants to bring his friend back. The “who” part tells me why Uta-napishtim is important. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “The most complete description of the flood story from the Babylonians is found in the Epic of Gilgamesh.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Where is the most complete Babylonian flood story found?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: Do you know an old story from your culture about water or a flood?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: What the Qur’an Says About His People
objectives: Describe how Noah’s people answered his warning.
Find the Qur’anic sources given in the chapter.
Explain the challenge at the end.
Use reporting verbs with their patterns.
content.pedagogy: The chapter is built from Qur’anic references. Learners list the people’s reactions (called him crazy → accused him of lying → threatened him → challenged him) and match each with its surah. The sources are read as they are, without extra comment.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The punishment was a warning from Allah, not Noah’s own wish.
The surah names are part of the text; they show where each idea comes from.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: warn someone (not) to · accuse someone of + -ing · threaten to · ask someone to · instead of + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): Noah warned his community not to worship …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *accused him to lie · *threatened stoning · *instead of think.
Use (Activity 4): listening before judging.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: SU-rah NÛH, zâ-ri-YÂT, NECM, şu-a-RÂ, KA-mer, HÛD.
Stress: re-BEL-lious, AC-cused, THREAT-ened.
beforeReading: Ask: “How do people sometimes react to a warning they do not like?”
duringReading: First reading: How did the people answer Noah?
Second reading: list the reactions and their sources.
Find what they asked Noah to do at the end.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Reactions and sources; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: listening before judging; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why do you think the people called Noah crazy?
What did the people challenge Noah to do?
Why is it important to think before we judge a message?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Surah Nûh” and “A Challenge” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: punishment, Instead of, right away, verses, threatened.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a chart: reaction / surah.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Report the people’s four reactions in four sentences with different reporting verbs.

formativeAssessment: Finds a source in the chapter.
expectedResponses: Noah warned his community not to worship anyone except Allah. Instead of thinking deeply, they accused him of lying and threatened to stone him to death.
content.transferTask: Write about why we should listen before we judge.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the reporting verb patterns correctly?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “accused … of” and one with “warned … not to”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain how Noah’s people answered his warning, using the surahs as evidence. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads up to “morally lost” and B reads the rest. Each explains the main idea. The partner names one surah from that part.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence with “Instead of”. Asker asks “What three things did they do?” Checker checks the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A friend asks, “How do we know what Noah’s people did?” The learner answers and names two surahs.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Finally, they challenged Noah and asked him to bring the punishment that he warned them about right away.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the Qur’an says about Noah’s people. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer give a surah and verse after almost every sentence?” (To show where each piece of information comes from.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give three actions of the people and name at least one surah.

thinkAloud.sentence: Instead of thinking deeply about Noah’s message, they called him crazy, accused him of lying, and threatened to stone him to death (Surah ash-Shu‘ara verse 116; Surah al-Qamar verse 9).
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Instead of” tells me what they did not do and what they did. They did not think deeply. They called him crazy, accused him and threatened him. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “According to Surah adh-Dhariyat verse 46 and Surah an-Najm verse 52, his people were very cruel, rebellious, and morally lost.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What three words describe his people?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: Why is it important to listen before we judge someone?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with an example.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Idols of Noah’s People
objectives: Explain how idol worship developed among Noah’s people.
Name the five idols.
Say what the people believed the idols could do.
Use although, however and eventually.
content.pedagogy: The chapter explains how respect for righteous men slowly turned into idol worship over generations. A step chart shows the change. The hadith and verse references are read as they are.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The five names were good and righteous men at first.
The statues were made to remember their good actions, not to worship them.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: although (contrast in one sentence) · however (contrast in a new sentence) · eventually · to + verb (purpose)
Notice (Activity 1): Although Prophet Noah invited them …, they believed …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the words, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Although …, but … · *However they forgot (no comma).
Use (Activity 4): remembering good people rightly.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ibn AB-bas, sa-HÂ-be, WAD, su-WA’, ya-GHUS, ya-’UK, NASR.
Stress: RIGHT-eous, e-VEN-tu-al-ly, in-SIST-ed.
beforeReading: Ask: “Why do people make statues of famous people?”
duringReading: First reading: How did idol worship develop?
Second reading: complete the step chart.
Find what the people believed about the idols.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Step chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: remembering good people rightly; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did people first make statues of the righteous men?
What changed in later generations?
Why is it important to remember the real story?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Ibn Abbas” and “Five Idols” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: companions, worshipped, insisted on, righteous, eventually, wealth.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the step chart with the first step written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph about how idol worship developed with although, however and eventually.

expectedResponses: Originally, Wad, Suwa’, Yaghus, Ya’uk and Nasr were good and righteous men. People made statues to remember them. However, later generations forgot the real story and eventually worshipped them.
content.transferTask: Write about how we can remember good people in the right way.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see how a small change grew over generations?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “although” and one with “however”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain how idol worship developed among Noah’s people. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 2 and B reads paragraph 3. Each explains the main idea. Together they write the steps in order.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the names of the five idols. Asker asks “What did the people believe the idols could do?” Checker finds the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A younger student asks, “Why did people make statues of good men?” The learner explains and says what went wrong later.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “This is how idol worship developed.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how statues of good men became idols. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What was the first purpose of the statues, and how did it change?” (To remember good actions; later generations forgot and worshipped them.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name the five idols and use “later” and “eventually” in the right order.

thinkAloud.sentence: However, later generations forgot the real story of the statues and eventually, they began worshipping them directly.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “However” shows a change. The statues were first for remembering. “Eventually” tells me the change happened slowly. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “According to the Qur’an, Noah’s people worshipped statues instead of Allah.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Which surah names the five idols?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: How can people remember good people without making statues?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one more idea.

objectives: Explain Noah’s arguments against idol worship.
Compare how the poor and the rich leaders answered.
Explain why Noah refused to send away the poor believers.
Use because, as, therefore, so and yet.
content.pedagogy: The longest chapter. It moves from Noah’s arguments (the balance of day and night, the sun and the moon) to the conflict with the elites, the 950 years and finally Allah’s command to build the ark. Divide the chapter into four parts: arguments → reactions → poor vs rich → the end of the call.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Noah’s arguments were based on thinking about creation, not on force.
The rich leaders rejected the message to keep their wealth and control, not because the message was unclear.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: because · as (= because) · therefore · so (that) · yet
Notice (Activity 1): Because Allah owns everything … Therefore, …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the linkers, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Because of they wanted · *Therefore Noah told (no comma) · *Yet, but …
Use (Activity 4): equal in dignity.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: SU-rah a’-RÂF, HÛD.
Stress: il-LOG-i-cal, DEM-on-strate, po-TEN-tial, en-SLAVE-ment, LA-bor-ers.
beforeReading: Ask: “What arguments can we use to explain that something is wrong?”
duringReading: First reading: What did Noah say about the idols?
Second reading: complete the four-part chart.
Find why Noah refused to send away the poor believers.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–13 First reading in four parts; 13–19 Four-part chart; 19–23 Quick Challenge; 23–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–42 Use: equal in dignity; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How did Noah use the sun and the moon in his arguments?
Why did the elites feel threatened?
Why did Noah refuse to reject the poor believers?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Blind Faith” and “The Elites” when the picture is in place.

Word Notes: illogical, demonstrate, blind faith, potential, enslavement, severe judgment, treated, beat, mocked, laborers, humble, modest, pointed out, Instead, conflict, debates, arguments, look down on, stand against.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the four-part chart with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short debate: two arguments of Noah and the leaders’ answers, in the words of the book.

formativeAssessment: Compares the poor and the rich leaders.
Uses a cause or result linker correctly.
expectedResponses: Noah explained that the balance of day and night shows Allah’s power. Therefore, worshipping handmade idols is illogical. The poor believed his message, yet the rich leaders rejected it because they wanted to keep their wealth.
content.transferTask: Write about why rich and poor people are equal in dignity.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners follow the four parts of the long chapter?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “therefore” and one with “as”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners summarize Noah’s mission from his first call to his prayer. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraphs 1 to 4, B reads paragraphs 5 to 8. Each summarizes the part in three sentences. The partner asks a follow-up question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 4. Asker asks “What did the rich leaders ask Noah (pbuh) to do?” Checker reads his answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A friend says, “Rich and poor people cannot share the same ideas.” The learner answers using Noah’s reply.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Noah (pbuh) never gave up inviting his people to Allah’s message and reminded them of His severe judgment.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Noah (pbuh) invited his people and why the elites rejected him. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why did the poor believe and the elites reject the message?” (The poor found hope and equality; the elites wanted to keep their wealth and control.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain why idols are “illogical” in Noah’s argument and give the elites’ reason.

thinkAloud.sentence: Because Allah owns everything in the heavens and the earth, there can only be one true Creator.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Because” gives the reason, and the main clause gives the conclusion. The next sentence starts with “Therefore”, so it adds a second conclusion: worshipping idols is illogical. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Allah sent Noah (pbuh) to guide his people with His message.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What did Noah (pbuh) say the balance of day and night shows?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: Why is it wrong to look down on people because they are poor?
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one example.

objectives: Describe how Noah built the ark.
Report how the leaders reacted.
Explain the sign that the flood was beginning.
Use the past perfect and reported questions.
content.pedagogy: The chapter contrasts Noah’s hard work and trust with the leaders’ mocking questions. Learners report the leaders’ questions and notice the past perfect. Never act out Noah; learners report the questions only.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Noah built the ark far from the sea by Allah’s command; it was not his own idea.
The sign was water overflowing from the earth, not the first rain.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past perfect (had built, had lost) · reported questions
Notice (Activity 1): Noah hurried to the ship he had built …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then report the questions.
Likely errors: *They asked why was he building · *he has lost his mind.
Use (Activity 4): working hard when others doubt you.
content.pronunciationFocus: Stress: hu-mil-i-A-tion, O-ver-flow (noun), o-ver-FLOW (verb), mi-RAC-u-lous-ly.
beforeReading: Ask: “What would people say if someone built a huge ship far from the sea?”
duringReading: First reading: How did the leaders react?
Second reading: underline the leaders’ questions.
Find the sign that the flood was beginning.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–16 The leaders’ questions; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: working hard when others doubt you; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the leaders laugh at Noah?
What did Noah answer?
What did Noah bring onto the ark?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “In the Middle of Nowhere” and “The Sign” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: humiliation, overflow, command, suffering.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frame: They asked Noah why he …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Report all of the leaders’ questions in reported speech.

formativeAssessment: Describes how Noah built the ark.
expectedResponses: Noah built the ark in a quiet place far from the sea. The leaders asked him why he was building a huge ship. When the water overflowed, he hurried to the ship he had built.
content.transferTask: Write about working hard when others doubt you.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners report the questions without acting out the prophet?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “had + past participle”.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes how Noah built the ark.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners tell how Noah (pbuh) built the ark and what the leaders said. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner reads the leaders’ questions and explains them to a partner. The partner says what the leaders thought about Noah (pbuh).
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 3. Asker asks “What was the sign that the flood would start?” Checker checks the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A neighbor laughs at a person who is doing something new. The learner tells the neighbor about Noah’s patience.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Noah (pbuh) replied: “Soon you will see who will face humiliation and suffering.”” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Noah (pbuh) built the ark and how the people reacted. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why are the leaders’ questions funny to them but not to the reader?” (The reader knows the flood is coming.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the sign of the flood and say what Noah (pbuh) took on board.

thinkAloud.sentence: “Noah, did you stop being a prophet to become a carpenter?”
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: This is not a real question. The leaders do not want an answer. They are laughing at Noah (pbuh). Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “When Noah (pbuh) finished building the ark, he started waiting for Allah’s command.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What was the sign that the flood was beginning?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences about a time people laughed at a good idea.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

objectives: Explain who did not get on the Ark.
Compare the different numbers given by scholars.
Explain that scholars have different ideas.
Use either, the majority of and some … others.
content.pedagogy: A short chapter. It shows that Noah’s own wife and son did not believe, and that scholars give different numbers for the believers on the Ark. Learners practice presenting different views without choosing one.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The scholars give three different numbers; the book does not say which one is right.
Noah’s wife and son chose not to believe; being family did not change that.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: either (negative) · neither … nor · the majority of · some … others
Notice (Activity 1): His son did not accept the faith either.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the words, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *did not accept too · *the majority people · *some … the others say.
Use (Activity 4): different opinions.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ibn AB-bas.
Stress: ma-JOR-i-ty, MEAN-while, SCHOL-ars.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do family members always share the same beliefs?”
duringReading: First reading: Who did not get on the Ark?
Second reading: list the three numbers and their sources.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–9 First reading; 9–14 Three numbers; 14–18 Quick Challenge; 18–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: different opinions; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why do you think Noah’s son chose to stay away from the believers?
Why do scholars give different numbers?
How can we present different views fairly?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “His Family” and “Different Ideas” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: rejected, scholars.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a chart: source / number.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short paragraph that presents the three views fairly.

formativeAssessment: Explains who did not get on the Ark.
Uses either or some … others correctly.
expectedResponses: Noah’s wife did not believe, and his son did not accept the faith either. Ibn Abbas said there were 80 believers, but some people said 72 and others say only 10.
content.transferTask: Write about a question on which people have different opinions.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners present the different numbers without choosing one?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “either” and one with “some … others”.

metadata.title: Noah B1 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Prophet Noah (pbuh)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 11 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected texts about history, ideas and values, and who can produce supported explanations and short reflections.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the story of Prophet Noah: his title and mission, the ancient flood stories, the beginning of idol worship, his call and the conflict with the elites, the ark, the flood, Ashura and his last advice, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 11 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a map, a date or a picture of the sea.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: a fact file, a story summary, reactions with sources, steps, arguments, a flow chart or a timeline.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: past simple passive · be known for / as · bear a name
Ch2: present simple for summaries · passive (were written, is told, is found)
Ch3: warn someone (not) to · accuse someone of + -ing · threaten to · ask someone to · instead of + -ing
Ch4: although (contrast in one sentence) · however (contrast in a new sentence) · eventually · to + verb (purpose)
Ch5: because · as (= because) · therefore · so (that) · yet
Ch6: past perfect (had built, had lost) · reported questions
Ch7: either (negative) · neither … nor · the majority of · some … others
Ch8: ask / call / order + object + to-infinitive · stop + -ing
Ch9: gerund as subject · preposition + gerund · was (not) allowed · could
Ch10: either … or · become + adjective · be free to · recommend + -ing
Ch11: preposition + -ing · -ing clause (telling them …) · more … than

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, people, places and key events.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: identify main ideas, sequences, reasons, contrasts and the sources the writer gives.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe events, explain ideas and give reasons.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: produce connected B1 paragraphs using evidence, linking words and chapter patterns.

valuesFocus: D12 Patience — Waiting calmly and not giving up.
D1 Justice — Treating all people as equal.
D10 Humility — Not thinking that you are better than others.
D3 Diligence — Working hard to finish a task.
languageFocus: Every one of the 11 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, picture cards, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.
Never draw or act out Prophet Noah or any prophet. Posters and panels show only the ark, the water, the land and the animals.
The Qur’an quotations, the surah references and the hadith belong to the teacher-approved text; they are read as they are, without extra comment, and the exercises do not change their words.
Chapter 2 presents the Epic of Gilgamesh as an ancient Babylonian account; present it in the words of the book, without comparing or judging.
Chapter 7 gives different numbers from scholars, and Chapter 9 says “according to a report”; present these as the book gives them.
Read the parts about the punishment and about Noah’s son calmly, in the words of the book.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Prophet Noah connects with questions every community faces today: how to treat rich and poor people equally, how to stay patient and how to be thankful.

themes.title: Equal dignity:
themes.description: Noah refused to send away his modest and faithful friends (Chapter 5). Discuss how communities can treat rich and poor people as equal.

themes.title: Shared human stories:
themes.description: Flood stories are found in very old tablets from Sumer and Babylon (Chapter 2). Discuss why many cultures share similar stories.

themes.title: Gratitude:
themes.description: The believers fasted on Ashura to thank Allah for saving them (Chapter 9). Discuss how people in different cultures show gratitude.

themes.title: Humility:
themes.description: Noah told his sons to stay away from being arrogant (Chapter 11). Discuss why humility matters in leadership today.

actions: Ask an older family member for one piece of good advice and write it down.
Find Mount Judi on a modern map.
Make a small poster about patience for your classroom.

One language pattern I noticed today, and what it does in the sentence, is …
One action I can take this week that shows a value from the chapter is …

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 11 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows patience, justice, humility and diligence. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Patience: Patience: Noah invited his people to worship Allah alone for 950 years and continued his mission (Chapters 1 and 5).
Justice: Justice: Noah completely refused to send his modest and faithful friends away (Chapter 5).
Humility: Humility: Noah told his sons to stay away from being arrogant (Chapter 11).
Diligence: Diligence: Noah worked hard day and night to build the ark (Chapter 6).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 11, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell someone at home in five sentences the story of Noah and the ark, in your home language or in English.
